# Overview

Concentration-response experiments are rarely a single clean series. Replicates
sit together in tanks, vials or plates; the whole experiment may be repeated on
different genotypes, in different seasons, or with different contaminants. Those
structures are not usually of interest in themselves, but ignoring them means
treating observations as independent when they are not.

`bayesnec` offers two distinct routes, and choosing between them is the first
decision to make:

- **group-level (hierarchical) terms** --- `ogl()`, `pgl()` and
  `(par | group)` --- which keep every observation in **one** fit and let the
  grouping shift parts of the curve;
- **fitting each level separately** --- `bnec_group()` --- which gives every
  level its own complete model set, and lets the *functional form* differ
  between levels.

They answer different questions, and they suit different data. This vignette
works through both, on the dataset each is actually suited to.


``` r
library(bayesnec)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
```

# Which kind of grouping is it?

The distinction that matters is whether the grouping sits **within** a
concentration or **across** it, because it decides which route applies.

**Within concentration.** Each group occurs at one concentration only ---
replicate tanks, vials, plates. The group cannot have its own
concentration-response curve, because it spans no concentrations. What it can do
is shift the response level up or down, and that is a **group-level term**.

**Across concentration.** Each group spans the whole concentration range ---
different chemicals, species, seasons. Every level *could* have its own curve,
and the question is usually whether it does. That is **`bnec_group()`**.

Both structures appear in the packaged data, which is why this vignette uses two
datasets rather than forcing one to serve both:


``` r
data(nassarius)
data(herbicide)
```

- `nassarius` has **tanks nested inside concentrations** --- each tank receives
  one dose --- which is the within-concentration case.
- `herbicide` has **seven herbicides each spanning the full concentration
  range**, which is the across-concentration case.

# Part 1: group-level terms, one fit

## The data, and why survival rather than growth

`nassarius` records survival and growth of snails exposed to contaminants, in
replicate tanks of six animals.


``` r
nassarius |>
  filter(contaminant == "A") |>
  count(tank, dose) |>
  head()
#>   tank dose n
#> 1  A-1 0.00 6
#> 2 A-10 0.02 6
#> 3 A-11 0.04 6
#> 4 A-12 0.04 6
#> 5 A-13 0.04 6
#> 6 A-14 0.08 6
```

We model **survival**, not the growth of the survivors. That is a deliberate
choice and worth being explicit about, because the alternative is a trap:


``` r
nassarius |>
  filter(contaminant == "A") |>
  group_by(dose) |>
  summarise(n = n(), dead = sum(alive == 0), pct_dead = round(100 * mean(alive == 0)))
#> # A tibble: 11 × 4
#>     dose     n  dead pct_dead
#>    <dbl> <int> <int>    <dbl>
#>  1  0       24     3       12
#>  2  0.01    18     1        6
#>  3  0.02    18     0        0
#>  4  0.04    18     1        6
#>  5  0.08    18     0        0
#>  6  0.16    18     0        0
#>  7  0.31    18     0        0
#>  8  0.63    18     0        0
#>  9  1.25    18     0        0
#> 10  2.5     18    15       83
#> 11 20       18    18      100
```

Mortality rises with dose and reaches 100% at the top concentration. Filtering
to `alive == 1` in order to model growth would discard those animals
**non-randomly** --- more of them at higher doses --- so the surviving growth
values at high concentration are a survivorship-selected sample, and the top of
the curve disappears entirely. That is precisely what the `hurdle_gamma` family
and `bnec_hurdle()` exist to avoid; see `vignette("example6")`.

Modelling survival sidesteps it completely: every exposed animal is in the
model, and the deaths are the response rather than a filter.


``` r
surv <- nassarius |>
  filter(contaminant == "A") |>
  group_by(tank, dose) |>
  summarise(suc = sum(alive), tot = n(), .groups = "drop")
head(surv)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   tank   dose   suc   tot
#>   <chr> <dbl> <int> <int>
#> 1 A-1    0        5     6
#> 2 A-10   0.02     6     6
#> 3 A-11   0.04     6     6
#> 4 A-12   0.04     6     6
#> 5 A-13   0.04     5     6
#> 6 A-14   0.08     6     6
```

Note that survival is not 6/6 in every control tank --- there is a little
baseline mortality --- which is a useful reminder that the control is estimated,
not assumed.

## `ogl()` --- an offset shared by a group

`ogl()` gives each level of the grouping its own intercept: the whole curve
shifts up or down, and its shape is unchanged. This is the right term when
tanks differ in overall condition but respond to the contaminant the same way.


``` r
fit_ogl <- bnec(suc | trials(tot) ~ crf(dose, model = "nec3param") + ogl(tank),
                data = surv, family = binomial(link = "identity"),
                iter = 5e3, chains = 3, seed = 17)
#> Error: Failed to fit model nec3param.
```

## `pgl()` --- the grouping affects every parameter

`pgl()` allows every curve parameter to vary by level. It is far more demanding
of the data: with 34 tanks and six animals each there is very little information
per tank about the *shape* of a curve that tank does not span.


``` r
fit_pgl <- bnec(suc | trials(tot) ~ crf(dose, model = "nec3param") + pgl(tank),
                data = surv, family = binomial(link = "identity"),
                iter = 5e3, chains = 3, seed = 17)
```

## `(par | group)` --- a named parameter varies

Where there is prior reason to expect one specific parameter to vary, name it.
This is the middle ground, and usually the honest one: it says what is expected
to differ instead of allowing everything to.


``` r
fit_par <- bnec(suc | trials(tot) ~ crf(dose, model = "nec3param") + (top | tank),
                data = surv, family = binomial(link = "identity"),
                iter = 5e3, chains = 3, seed = 17)
```

## Priors for the group-level standard deviations

The `bayesnec` default priors are built for the curve parameters, not for
group-level standard deviations, so those fall through to the `brms` defaults.
Check what a formula will produce before fitting it:


``` r
check_formula(bayesnecformula(suc | trials(tot) ~ crf(dose, "nec3param") +
                                ogl(tank)),
              data = surv, run_par_checks = TRUE)
#> suc | trials(tot) ~ crf(dose, "nec3param") + ogl(tank)
```

## Failure modes, and being honest about them

Hierarchical structure on non-linear parameters is easy to write and hard to
identify. The caution in the `bayesnec` JSS article [@Fisher2024] applies
directly: a group-level term that the data cannot support does not announce
itself as an error --- it appears as a wide posterior, a divergent transition
count that creeps up, or a group-level standard deviation whose posterior looks
like its prior.

Check all three:


``` r
check_sampling(fit_ogl)
#> Error: object 'fit_ogl' not found
```


``` r
check_priors(fit_ogl)
```

If the group-level standard deviation's posterior is indistinguishable from its
prior, the grouping is not supported by the data and the term is adding
uncertainty without adding information. Drop it and say so, rather than keeping
it because it is more sophisticated.

# Part 2: fitting each level separately

Where each level spans the whole concentration range, the question changes: not
"does this group shift the response" but "does this group have a different
curve". `herbicide` is that case --- seven herbicides, each across the full
range.


``` r
herbicide |>
  group_by(herbicide) |>
  summarise(concentrations = n_distinct(concentration), n = n())
#> # A tibble: 7 × 3
#>   herbicide   concentrations     n
#>   <chr>                <int> <int>
#> 1 ametryn                  8    96
#> 2 atrazine                 7    84
#> 3 diuron                   6    72
#> 4 hexazinone               7    76
#> 5 irgarol                  6    72
#> 6 simazine                 6    72
#> 7 tebuthiuron              9   108
```

Note `fvfm` is a proportion with observations at or beyond the 0/1 boundary, so
`check_data()` applies its boundary handling for the `Beta` family --- see
`vignette("example1")`.


``` r
fit_grp <- bnec_group(fvfm ~ crf(log(concentration), model = "decline"),
                      data = herbicide, group_var = "herbicide",
                      family = Beta(link = "identity"),
                      iter = 5e3, chains = 3, seed = 17)
#> Error in expand_manec(mod_fits, formula = formulas, x_range = x_range, : None of the models fit successfully, try using bnec with a single model (e.g. ecxexp) using the default settings as a starting point for trouble shooting, or check ?show_params to make sure you have the correct parameter names for your priors.
```


``` r
fit_grp
#> Error: object 'fit_grp' not found
```

The family is chosen **once**, from the whole response, and passed down. Chosen
per level it could differ between levels, and the levels would no longer be
comparable.

## Crossed model weights


``` r
crossed_group_weights(fit_grp)
#> Error: object 'fit_grp' not found
```

Two readings, and they answer different questions. The **unrestricted** maximum
picks the best model for each level independently, and will typically assign
different equations to different levels --- that is the direct answer to whether
the functional form differs. The **diagonal** asks which single equation best
describes every level, restricted to models that every level actually fitted.

## Comparing the fitted curves

The weights say which *equation* fits each level. They do not say whether the
levels differ in the quantity being reported. For that, compare the posteriors
directly:


``` r
comp <- compare_posterior(fit_grp, comparison = "fitted")
#> Error: object 'fit_grp' not found
```


``` r
ggplot(comp$posterior_data, aes(x = x, y = Estimate)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Q2.5, ymax = Q97.5, fill = model), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = model)) +
  labs(x = "log(concentration)", y = "Predicted fv/fm",
       fill = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
#> Error: object 'comp' not found
```

`comp$prob_diff` gives the probability that one level's fitted curve exceeds
another's at each concentration, which is the quantity a reader usually wants
when asking whether two chemicals differ:


``` r
head(comp$prob_diff)
#> Error: object 'comp' not found
```

The two summaries can disagree, and that is informative rather than
contradictory. Two levels can favour the same equation while their curves sit
well apart, and two levels can favour different equations while their fitted
curves overlap almost entirely. Report both.

The levels are fitted independently and share no parameters, so the posteriors
are independent and these probabilities are read directly, with no
multiple-comparison adjustment implied.

**One caveat on reproducibility.** `compare_posterior()` pairs draws across
fits by permutation, and that permutation is not currently seeded --- see
issue #218. Re-running the comparison will move the third decimal place. Set a
seed for the fits themselves, and treat the comparison as indicative at that
precision.

# Choosing between the two routes

| | group-level term | `bnec_group()` |
|---|---|---|
| grouping sits | within a concentration | across concentrations |
| curve shape | shared | may differ by level |
| information | shared across groups | none shared |
| answers | does the group shift the response | does the group have a different curve |
| cost | needs enough groups to estimate a standard deviation | needs enough data *per level* for a whole model set |

A grouping that spans concentrations can technically be fitted either way, and
the choice is then about what is being asked. If the levels are a nuisance ---
plates, batches, seasons --- a group-level term is right, and sharing
information across them is the point. If the levels are the subject of the
analysis --- chemicals, species, treatments --- fitting them separately is
right, and sharing information between them would blur the very contrast being
tested.

What should not happen is choosing by convenience. Both routes are cheap to fit;
only one of them answers the question asked.
